q-129329.name: Question 1
q-129329.worked_solution:
Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{3x-2y+1}.
$$

The function $f(x,y)$ is continuous for all values of $x$ and $y.$ So, we can calculate the limit by substituting $(1,-2)$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,-2)}\sqrt[3]{3x-2y+1} & =\sqrt[3]{3(1)-2(-2)+1} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{3+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{8} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

$$

q-74924.name: Question 6
q-74924.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (2,2,-1)}\frac{xyz-z{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}=\frac{2\cdot 2\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot {2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,2,-1)}\frac{xyz-z{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,2,-1)}\frac{yz(x-y)}{-(x-y)(x+y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,2,-1)}\frac{yz}{-x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,2,-1)}\frac{yz}{-x-y} & =\frac{2\cdot (-1)}{-2-2} \\  & =\frac{-2}{-4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{y+z}{\sqrt{x-y}-\sqrt{x+z}} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{(y+z)(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})}{(\sqrt{x-y}-\sqrt{x+z})(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{(y+z)(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})}{(x-y)-(x+z)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{(y+z)(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})}{-(y+z)} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{\cancel{(y+z)}(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})}{\cancel{(y+z)}} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0,1)}\frac{x+y-{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{x+y}-z} & =\frac{1+0-{1}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+0}-1} \\  & =\frac{1+0-1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}

q-74967.name: Question 16
q-74967.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=\frac{2\cdot {0}^{2}}{2\cdot {0}^{2}-{0}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{2{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the line $y=0$ (the $x$-axis),  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=0}\,\frac{2{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2\cdot {0}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{0}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$

q-74968.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{xy}{2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}}=\frac{0\cdot 0}{2\cdot {0}^{2}+3\cdot {0}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{xy}{2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}+3{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{5{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the line $y=-x$,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=-x}\,\frac{xy}{2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{-{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}+3{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{-{x}^{2}}{5{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,(-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{xy}{2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$

q-36139.name: Question 18
q-36139.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y}
$$

I. The limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{3}$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$

II. The limit evaluates to $-1$ along the path $y=-{x}^{2}$

III. The limit exists and is equal to $\frac{1}{3}$
q-36139.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y}=\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+2\cdot 0}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=-{x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=-{x}^{2}}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2(-{x}^{2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{-{x}^{2}}{-{x}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y}=\text{DNE}
$$

q-129403.name: Question 19
q-129403.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =\frac{{0}^{2}-{0}^{2}}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0-0}{0+0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=0}\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}-{0}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{0}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$
